1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.strategy: Closes the centre and claims space at once, taking the f6 square away from Black's king's knight. White gets a cramping pawn and a clear space edge; Black gets a sound structure, a light-squared bishop that can still develop outside the pawn chain, and a pawn break against the base of White's chain.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.background: For many years regarded as inferior, chiefly after Nimzowitsch, as White, was strategically outplayed by Capablanca at New York 1927. In the 21st century it became the most popular line against the Caro–Kann.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: The classical move: White develops a piece, defends e4 and prepares to recapture on e4 with the knight if Black takes it. The game stays open, with White aiming at freer development and Black relying on a sound structure and an active light-squared bishop.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.name: Caro–Kann Defence

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2.strategy: Prepares to recapture on e4 with the knight, like 3.Nc3, but keeps the c-pawn free to support d4 and so meets a fianchetto calmly. The cost is a knight that blocks the c1-bishop, so White's development is a little less harmonious.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2.background: Its popularity rose in the 1970s as a way to avoid Bukhuti Gurgenidze's 3...g6 against 3.Nc3.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Resolves the central tension at once. Black recaptures with the c-pawn and the centre becomes symmetrical, with the pawn majorities on opposite wings: White's on the queenside, Black's on the kingside. A quieter game in which White hopes for a small edge.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn, aiming for a broad pawn centre if Black takes. The price is slowness: the pawn takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the a7–g1 diagonal. Black can build up solidly against the dark squares or accept the challenge.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Maróczy Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3.background: Also called the Fantasy Variation and the Tartakower Variation. Alexander Morozevich, ranked second in the world in July 2008, has played it with success.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4 but does nothing for e4: after ...dxe4 the pawn attacks the knight, so White has no immediate recapture and loses time regaining the pawn. Black gets an easy game.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a piece, but the bishop is the one that ends up on e4 after ...dxe4, and ...Nf6 then hits it. Black develops with tempo and takes the initiative.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Be3.strategy: A gambit: after ...dxe4 White plays f3 to open lines and offers a pawn for a lead in development. The compensation is doubtful, so Black can take the pawn and defend with care.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Be3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Mieses Gambit

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3 Nf6.strategy: Natural development, but it invites 4.e5 at once, which drives the knight back with a gain of space. Taking on e4 is the cleaner answer to the bishop move; this lets White into a pleasant space-gaining game.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5.strategy: Brings the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, the main idea of the defence. White has more space, Black a solid structure and the ...c5 break against d4; the bishop is undefended on f5, which White tries to exploit.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5.strategy: Attacks the base of White's pawn chain at once. If White takes on c5, the pawn on e5 loses its support and Black can usually win the pawn back, though the light-squared bishop has a harder time getting out. A sharp, less travelled alternative to the main line.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Botvinnik-Carls Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5.background: Named after Carl Carls, who played one of its earliest appearances at Breslau in 1912, and Mikhail Botvinnik, who relied on it in his 1961 rematch with Tal; it had remained uncommon until then. Botvinnik won the match but scored two draws and a loss with it. New in Chess also called it the Arkell–Khenkin Variation, after the work of Keith Arkell and Igor Khenkin on it.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5.strategy: The thematic recapture: it frees the c6 square for the knight and leaves Black with an easy, solid game. The centre is symmetrical, but the pawn majorities lie on opposite wings, White's on the queenside and Black's on the kingside.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn and invites White to recapture with the f-pawn, which gives White a broad centre and a half-open f-file but loosens its own king's position. A more adventurous reply than the solid ...e6: Black opens the game and challenges the centre at once.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Releases the tension and denies White the broad two-pawn centre and frees d5 for Black's pieces. Black gets a flexible, solid structure and a bishop that can come out before the pawns close it in.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and pressure d4, keeping the d5 tension instead of exchanging. Black allows White to take space in the centre and on the kingside, but builds a counterattack on the long diagonal against the white centre.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Gurgenidze System
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.background: Originated by Bukhuti Gurgenidze, this variation led to a rise in the popularity of 3.Nd2 during the 1970s.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the tension, hoping for a quiet game. White can drive the knight back with a pawn, gaining space and a closed centre for which Black may not have prepared, so Black ends up passive for little.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Campomanes Attack

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 b5.strategy: Hopes to drive the knight from c3 with ...b4, but loosens the queenside and spends a move on a pawn. White stops the idea with a3 and keeps a lead in development, so Black is left with weaknesses; it works only as a surprise at club level.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 b5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Gurgenidze Counterattack

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 dxe4.strategy: The principal answer: Black takes the e-pawn and settles the tension in the centre at once. White's knight must recapture on e4, where Black can challenge it, while Black's pawn structure stays healthy; the price is that White gets slightly more space and the first go at development.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 Qb6.strategy: Attacks the d4 pawn, which the knight on d2 has cut off from the queen. White simply defends it, and the early queen sortie has then cost Black time in the race for development without creating a lasting weakness: playable, but second-best here.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 Qb6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Edinburgh Variation

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn with a gain of time, because the pawn on e4 attacks the knight. White has no knight that can recapture at once and must spend moves to win the pawn back; Black has to keep it defended and develop quickly for the extra pawn to count.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3 Nf6 4.e5.strategy: Gains space with tempo, driving the knight back. The pawn has left e4, so the bishop on d3 now looks along the diagonal towards h7. White gets an advance structure in which the bishop is already well placed, and Black has to retreat the knight and start working against the pawn chain.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7.strategy: The natural retreat: from d7 the knight attacks the pawn on e5 and prepares to challenge the chain. The cost is that the knight blocks the c8-bishop, so Black's development is cramped for the moment, and White can try to exploit that at once.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.e6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Mieses Attack, Landau Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Bd3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.e6.strategy: A trap gambit: the pawn attacks f7 and d7, and taking it with the f-pawn loses by force (Qh5+ g6, Bxg6+ hxg6, Qxg6 mate). Against careful play it is only a pawn given away, so the idea works as a trap rather than as an opening plan.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nf3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Short Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nf3.background: The line 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2 c5 6.Be3 was popularised by the English grandmaster Nigel Short and was often seen in the 1990s.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nf3.strategy: The patient main line: White develops and keeps the space advantage without committing the pawns. The knight guards d4, so a ...c5 break can be met by recapturing there; Black must either break at once or settle for a cramped but solid position.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3.background: A popular line in the 1980s that the Latvian grandmaster Alexei Shirov later favoured; it is sometimes called the Shirov Attack.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3.strategy: A sharp idea with the knight first: Nc3 takes e4 away from the bishop, so that a pawn storm on the kingside can drive it back without letting it out to e4. Developing a piece before attacking makes this better founded than the direct pawn thrusts.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3.strategy: Reinforces d4 with a pawn, so the ...c5 break meets a solid chain rather than a loose centre. The price is that the b1-knight loses its best square; White builds up slowly and aims for a lasting space advantage.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.g4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Bayonet Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.g4.strategy: The most direct attack on the bishop: White gains kingside space and drives it back, but commits pawns to the kingside before a single piece is developed. The weakened king's side gives Black targets, so the game turns sharp.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Ne2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Bronstein Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Ne2.strategy: Heads for g3 to hit the bishop and keeps the c-pawn free to support d4. But it is slow and it obstructs the king's bishop, and Black can calmly build the usual structure and give the bishop a retreat.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Tal Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4.strategy: Prepares g4 to trap the bishop, and a careless reply loses it: 4...e6 5.g4 wins a piece. Black has simple ways to give the bishop an escape square, after which the early h-pawn advance has only weakened White's kingside.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.b4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Prins Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.b4.strategy: Takes the c5 square away from Black's pawn break, but develops nothing and loosens White's own queenside. It neither challenges the bishop nor adds to the centre, so Black carries on developing and can hit the b4 pawn with ...a5.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3 e6.strategy: Black's key move in this structure: it supports d5, gives the dark-squared bishop room and prepares the ...c5 break, while the bishop on f5 stays safely outside the chain.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6.strategy: Black's main reply: it supports d5, frees the dark-squared bishop and prepares the ...c5 break, accepting that the bishop on f5 will soon be attacked. Black meets the pawn storm calmly, with a solid structure and counterplay against White's centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 Qb6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack, Dreyev Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 Qb6.strategy: Meets the sharp set-up with counterplay: the queen eyes the d4 and b2 pawns, so White must spend time defending. The cost is that the queen is exposed to harassment and ...e6 is delayed, so Black's structure stays loose.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3 e6 5.Be2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Advance, Short Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3 e6 5.Be2.strategy: A quiet developing move that readies castling. White chooses e2 rather than d3, so Black's active bishop cannot simply be exchanged for it, and keeps the space edge while d4 stays well defended if the centre opens.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once and starts the pawn storm. The knight on c3 covers e4, so the bishop has few good retreats. White gets space and attacking chances at the price of an airy king's side, and the game is sharp, with Black striking back in the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 B.strategy: The natural retreat: from g6 the bishop stays on the b1–h7 diagonal and remains a lively piece, instead of being driven off the board. The cost is that it can become a target for the h-pawn, which White uses to gain more space.

Develops without blocking the f-pawn and prepares to push the h-pawn at the bishop, while the knight can also head for f4. White commits to the kingside attack and leaves the centre to be defended by pawns.

Strikes at White's centre at once, before the pawn storm bites: a counterattack in the centre is the best answer to a flank attack. White's h-pawn push threatens to trap the bishop, so Black has to play accurately and the game is sharp.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops and prevents ...Bf5: the bishop on f5 would simply be taken. The main line of the exchange gives White a slightly freer game in a quiet, strategic fight, while Black has to develop accurately to stay level.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4.background: Named after Vasily Panov and the world champion Mikhail Botvinnik.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4.strategy: Hits the d5 pawn at once and invites an isolated queen's pawn: White accepts the long-term weakness of d4 for quick development, a grip on e5 and attacking chances on the kingside. A sharp, open game in which White must keep the initiative.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bf4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bf4.strategy: Gets the bishop outside the pawn chain, eyeing b8 and e5. But it does nothing to stop ...Bf5, so Black simply develops and White has no more than a symmetrical position.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4, but does not stop Black's c8-bishop from coming out to f5, where it is active. Black develops without difficulty and equalises comfortably.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.g4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation, Bulla Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.g4.strategy: A pawn thrust on the flank before a single piece is developed. It claims kingside space but loosens White's own king's side and does nothing about the centre, and ...Nf6 hits the pawn at once with the bishop on c8 behind it.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6.strategy: The natural point of the recapture on d5: the knight develops with pressure on d4 and eyes e5. Black asks White to support the pawn and sets up a solid position, accepting a slightly less comfortable game for safety.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6.strategy: The principal reply: the knight develops, protects d5 and eyes e4. Black lets White build the Panov set-up and plans to blockade and target the d4 pawn if it becomes isolated.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and keeps the choice of set-up open, but delays ...Nf6, so White can sometimes steer for other positions. A respectable move order that mostly leads to the same structures.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nf3 Nc6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight and adds pressure on d4, while the c8-bishop stays free to choose its square. The structure is stable, d4 and d5 facing each other, so development and piece play decide the game rather than a pawn break.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5..strategy: Supports d4 with a pawn and takes b4 from the knight, so ...Nb4 cannot harass the bishop. It also opens the diagonal for the queen towards b3, giving White a solid centre and extra pressure on Black's queenside.

Develops the last central piece, adds a defender to d5 and controls e4, so White cannot easily occupy the centre. Black keeps the structure solid and stays ready to bring the light-squared bishop out actively.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Exchange Variation, Rubinstein Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5..strategy: Places the bishop outside the pawn chain, where it covers e5 and the b8–h2 diagonal. White plays for a small, lasting edge from the more harmonious piece placement, and Black needs accurate development to stay level.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Piles up on d5 with the knight: with both c4 and Nc3 attacking it, Black must keep it defended. White develops with a purpose and prepares to open the centre by capturing on d5 when it suits.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Modern Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Adds a second defender to d5 and completes the knight development. Black keeps pressure on d4 with the knight on c6, so White must decide how to keep the centre together.

Develops the bishop against the knight that guards d5. If the knight is exchanged, Black either gets doubled pawns or loses a key defender of d5, so Black has to meet the threat with care. White plays for a sharp, open game.
A calm developing move that adds a defender to d4, which the knight on c6 presses, and prepares castling. White keeps all options open and lets Black decide between a sharp and a solid set-up.

Gives d5 a third defender and releases the dark-squared bishop. The cost is a passive light-squared bishop on c8. Black aims for a solid set-up in which the d5 pawn is safe and White's initiative has to be earned.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Modern Defence, Mieses Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Pins the knight against the queen and adds pressure on d4, because the knight on f3 is its defender. The sharpest reply: Black plays for tactics based on the pinned knight and for damage to White's pawn structure.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Modern Defence, Carlsbad Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: The solid answer: it adds a defender to d5 and opens the f8-bishop, and the pin on f6 is harmless, since Black can retake there with the queen or the g-pawn. Black keeps a sound centre and develops without concessions.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Modern Defence, Czerniak Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Pins the knight on c3 against the king, so it cannot take on d5, and hits the centre from the side. The queen is exposed on a5, though, so Black must keep the initiative: White can unpin and carry on with the development.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Modern Defence, Reifir-Spielmann Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Attacks d4 for a second time and the undefended b2 pawn, so White has to react at once instead of developing. Black invites sharp play with the queen out early; the double pressure brings counterplay, but the knight on f6 stays under the bishop's fire.

Takes the pawn at once, but it cannot be kept: the bishop retakes it, and Black has given up the central tension for little. White then stands freer, with quicker development and the pin on f6 still in place.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Adds a second attacker against d5 and develops a piece, so Black has to decide at once how to hold the pawn. White is ready to accept an isolated d4 pawn later in return for quick development and kingside chances, so the game becomes a fight over the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.c.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Gunderam Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.c.strategy: Pushes past d5 to take space on the queenside, where the pawn controls b6 and d6. It also gives up the pressure on d5 that makes the Panov dangerous, and the far-advanced pawn can be undermined, so Black reaches a comfortable game without having to defend its centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: The solid reply: it adds a defender to d5 and opens the f8-bishop. Black accepts a slightly passive set-up for a sound structure and meets White's initiative with piece play against d4, a pawn that often ends up isolated once the centre is resolved.

The ambitious reply: the knight pressures d4 and keeps the e-pawn free, so Black counterattacks White's centre instead of only defending d5. The cost is that d5 is held by pieces alone and White can aim at it at once, so Black must be ready for a sharper fight.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Fianchetto Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and press on d4 from a distance, but leaves d5 to be exchanged: White takes it and Black has to win the pawn back with its pieces. A more active set-up than ...e6, bought with a less sturdy centre.

The natural development: it guards d4 and controls e5 while keeping the pressure on d5, so Black must decide how to meet the tension. White aims for a lead in development and an open centre, with the isolated d4 pawn as the structural price if the centre is resolved.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Main Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Pins the knight on c3 against the king, so the piece that attacks d5 can neither take there nor move away. Black also threatens to double White's pawns with ...Bxc3, trading the bishop for a knight to take the sting out of the pressure on d5.

Takes the pawn before Black's fianchetto is ready. The pawn on d5 is attacked twice and defended once, so Black will win it back, and White should expect an open game with an isolated d4 pawn in return for active pieces.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Panov Attack, Fianchetto Defence, Fianchetto Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: A gambit of time: Black develops the bishop and prepares castling instead of recapturing at once. The d5 pawn stays attacked twice and defended once, so White must spend a move to hold it; if White manages, Black has given a pawn for little.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4.strategy: Recaptures with the f-pawn to build a full pawn centre and open the f-file for the rook, the idea behind 3.f3. The price is a weaker king: the e1–h4 diagonal is open and the e4 pawn is a target, so White has to play actively.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 e5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, attacking d4 with pawn and queen while White's king lacks its f-pawn. The sharpest answer: Black gives up a modest set-up for an open game in which both kings are exposed and White's lead in development has to be met accurately.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 e5 5.Nf.strategy: Develops with an attack on e5, meeting Black's central strike with piece pressure instead of settling the tension. Black has nothing to defend e5 yet, so it must exchange or support the pawn, while White keeps the better development.

Takes on d4 and opens the centre, but leaves the king in the middle and hands White the initiative. The extra pawn is only borrowed: d4 is attacked twice, and the open diagonals against f7 and the open f-file make delay dangerous.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 e5 5.Nf.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Maróczy Variation, Maróczy Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 e5 5.Nf.strategy: Develops with an eye on f7 instead of retaking on d4 at once. The pawn is still attacked twice and defended once, so Black must keep it while finishing development, and White plays for the initiative against an uncastled king.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: Recaptures with the knight and reaches exactly the position that 3.Nc3 leads to, so the move order changes nothing. The knight is well placed on e4, eyeing c5, d6, f6 and g5, and White has the freer game while Black must find a way to challenge it.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.Ng5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Ulysses Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.Ng5.strategy: Hits the pawn on e4 at once and offers a gambit: if Black holds the pawn with a developing move, White has to prove that the lead in development is worth it. Playable, but the knight on g5 is easily challenged and the pawn is real.
